newsitem.title: USA: Delta overhauls Atlantic, European routes.
newsitem.headline: Delta overhauls Atlantic, European routes.

text.p: Delta Air Lines Inc. Tuesday announced plans to overhaul its trans-Atlantic and intra-European flights to bolster profits, and said it will take a $60 million one-time restructuring charge in the first quarter.

The changes, aimed at boosting Delta's annual operating income by $62 million, will result in 600 to 800 job cuts in Frankfurt, Germany and additional lay-offs in Bucharest, Romania; St. Petersburg, Russia and Warsaw, Poland.
Atlanta-based Delta had operating profits of $463 million in the year ended June 30.

Under the plan, Delta will add domestic and European flights from New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport, discontinue service to certain European cities and restructure its operations in Frankfurt.

By the summer, the company will have 245 weekly trans-Atlantic flights to 26 European cities, it said. Delta already serves more European cities nonstop than any other U.S. airline, and last year carried 91 million passengers worldwide, more than any other carrier.
Delta said it will immediately begin talks with employees in European cities affected by the changes.
"Regrettably, as we discontinue the intra-European flights from Frankfurt, we must also balance the number of people with the new level of Delta flying," said Ronald Allen, Delta's chairman.

Delta will discontinue intra-Europe service from Frankfurt to six cities and stop trans-Atlantic service to Frankfurt from three U.S. cities. Delta will continue daily service from Frankfurt to Bombay.

Delta said it will end its flights linking Frankfurt with Athens, Bucharest, Istanbul, Warsaw, Moscow and St. Petersburg. Service on these routes was severely constrained by international regulations, resulting in empty seats and marginal profits, Delta said.

Allen said Delta's plan was to strengthen its "position as the No. 1 jet air carrier at JFK airport, the largest and most important European gateway, and build on our leadership as the No. 1 U.S. air carrier across the North Atlantic."
Delta will remain the largest U.S. carrier in Germany, he said. Delta operations over the North Atlantic are already profitable, and become more so with the changes, he said.

Analysts said Delta's plan was aimed at fixing problems dating back to its $1.2 billion acquisition of Pan Am's European routes in 1991, and the changes would only succeed if the airline could also quickly improve its service and upgrade its fleet.
"Now that they've got the schedule and routes in shape, they need to improve the fleet and the product. But they recognise the urgency of this," said Samuel Buttrick, analyst at PaineWebber Inc.
Delta's international business class service and amenities are among the worst in the industry, analysts said.
Delta said it will announce an overhaul of its trans-Atlantic premium class services within the next four or five weeks.
"That will give them in-flight product that is consistent with their market presence. You don't want to be offering the most flights with the worst service," Buttrick said.
Delta also said it will make a "major decision" for aircraft purchases within the next 60 days.
Delta is evaluating the Airbus Industrie 330, Boeing Co.'s 777 or the Boeing 767-400 as possible replacements for its fleet of ageing Lockheed L-1011s.
Under the restructuring, Delta will add a daily flight from Atlanta to Stuttgart, Germany, and a second daily flight from Atlanta to Zurich, Switzerland.
Delta said it will start daily flights to JFK from Houston, Philadelphia and Seattle and add a third daily flight to JFK from Los Angeles.

The company said it will add new nonstop service from JFK to Istanbul, Turkey; Madrid, Spain and Manchester, England, as well as extend existing seasonal service to Athens, Greece year-round and add a second, seasonal daily flight to Rome.
Delta's stock rose $2.50 to $72.375 on the New York Stock Exchange in late trading.
